title: Basic Theorems on Limits of Algebraic Functions
topicTitle: Limits and continuity: limits of a function, indeterminate forms, algebraic properties of limits (without proof), basic theorems on limits of algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
notes: **Polynomial limit theorem:** For any polynomial $p(x)$, $\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = p(a)$. Simply substitute $x = a$.
**Rational function theorem:** For a rational function $r(x) = p(x)/q(x)$, if $q(a) \neq 0$, then $\lim_{x \to a} r(x) = p(a)/q(a)$. Direct substitution works.
**When direct substitution fails ($0/0$ form):** Factor the numerator and denominator, cancel common factors, then substitute.
**Limits at infinity for polynomials:** $\lim_{x \to \infty} a_nx^n + \cdots = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } a_n > 0 \\ -\infty & \text{if } a_n < 0 \end{cases}$ (for $n \geq 1$).

**Limits at infinity for rational functions:** Divide every term by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator. If degree of numerator < degree of denominator, limit = 0. If equal, limit = ratio of leading coefficients.
**Nested radicals:** For $\lim_{x \to a} (\sqrt{f(x)} - L)$ type limits, rationalize by multiplying by the conjugate $\sqrt{f(x)} + L$.
confusion: For rational functions where both numerator and denominator approach 0 at $x = a$, do NOT simply say the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients — you must factor and simplify first.
At infinity, only the highest-degree terms matter. Lower-degree terms become negligible.
universalFacts: For polynomials and rational functions, the first strategy is always direct substitution. Only when it fails do you need algebraic manipulation.
The degree comparison rule for limits at infinity is a quick diagnostic tool that avoids unnecessary computation.
